newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium to head into EMU by hook or by crook.
newsitem.headline: Belgium to head into EMU by hook or by crook.

text.p: Belgium will on Tuesday be doing what other European countries have done before it -- announcing a budget which will ensure that it will be in Europe's 1999 single currency union by hook or by crook.

Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene will present the 1997 budget to parliament on Tuesday afternoon, but economists said on Monday it was clear that only some of the measures to be taken would help reduce the budget deficit structurally.
Elements of the budget have already emerged, including the sum of 80 billion Belgian francs ($2.55 billion) covering a package of increases in indirect taxes and spending cuts.
Economists said it contained a number of one-off measures, taken in part to avoid any drastic cuts in heavy spending areas such as social security, which would be hugely unpopular.

News that 50 billion francs of spending cuts are to fall in the social security sector has already brought angered workers on to the streets and on Monday the CGSP public services union called for further protests.

Financial markets were split on the budget leaks with the bond market welcoming the package which, the government says, will bring the budget deficit down to below three percent of gross domestic product.
The three percent threshold is part of the criteria in the Maastricht Treaty on economic and monetary union (EMU).

In the share market, however, dealers said there was some concern that the Dehaene cabinet was not doing enough to tackle the problems of the budget deficit and the state debt. At over 130 percent of GDP the latter is the highest in Europe.

Economists said the use of non-recurrent measures to raise revenues or cut spending would not become a hurdle for Belgium's entry into the currency union, particularly because other European countries, notably France, had adopted a similar approach to their budget problems.
"Most European countries are trying to cure a hangover by having another drink," said economist Christer Lindholm at J.P. Morgan in Brussels.
"At one stage the hangover is going to come back and it is going to be gruesome," he said.

A major headache in Belgium is social security spending, which as a percentage of GDP has remained relatively steady over the last 15 years, while government layouts in other areas have been pruned, economists said.
They said the proposed 50 billion franc cut in social spending in the 1997 budget was a step in the right direction.
Kristine Vandenbergen, economist at BBL, said there were some structural measures in the budget.

"Dehaene has shown which is the way to go," she said, adding the Prime Minister had learnt an important political lesson from France where an attempt at wholesale reforms last year sparked wide-ranging protests.

Social security reform "is as necessary in Belgium as almost everywhere else in Europe, but it is going to be postponed for as long as possible," Lindholm said. "At one stage they will have to do something."

He said that on the basis of what was known about the 1997 budget it was politically "very good" since the Maastricht criteria would be met and it contained hardly any controversial or politically sensitive measures.

Dehaene is likely to tell parliament on Tuesay that in view of a rapidly ageing population he is addressing a time bomb by reforming the pensions system through a gradual increase in the retirement age for women to that for men and taxing all early retirement offers.

He is expected to claim there is a form of social justice in the budget since banks will have to pay a tax on the amount outstanding in savings deposit accounts, now tax-free, which are Belgium's most popular savings schemes.
The tax would hit the accounts of the rich harder than those of the poor.

Some of the measures, Dehaene will say, will be for Belgians' own good. These include higher taxes on drinking, which will lead supporters to say he is curing a hangover by raising the price of beer and spirits.
